anchorChartsIntro: Start with the seven Midterm focus skills. Each chart has a poster, a how-to guide, five worked examples, and a quick check. The supporting charts after them cover drama, text evidence, and vocabulary in context. These are original study guides that supplement your classroom charts.

anchorCharts.name: Author's Purpose
anchorCharts.body: The author's purpose is the main reason a text was written. Most texts persuade, inform, or entertain (P.I.E.); some also explain how or why, or describe so you can picture something. Look at the whole text, not one sentence, and ask: What does the author want me to think, know, or feel?

guide.label: Persuade · 說服
guide.text: Convince the reader to believe or do something. Clues: an opinion, reasons, evidence, words like should, must, best, never.

guide.label: Inform · 告知
guide.text: Teach facts about a real topic. Clues: facts, numbers, dates, headings, diagrams, captions.

guide.label: Entertain · 娛樂
guide.text: Tell a story or share something fun or exciting. Clues: characters, a problem, dialogue, humor, suspense. Stories, plays, and most poems.

guide.label: Explain · 說明
guide.text: Show how something works or why it happens, often in steps or cause-and-effect order. A special kind of informing.

guide.label: Describe · 描寫
guide.text: Help the reader picture a person, place, or thing with sensory details (see, hear, smell, touch, taste).

steps: Preview: genre, title, headings, pictures. A play or poem is usually written to entertain; an article usually informs.
Read and collect clues: opinions and reasons, facts and numbers, or characters and events.
Name ONE main purpose and support it with two details from the text.
Ask what else the author does: an article can also persuade at the end; a story can also teach a lesson.
anchorCharts.tip: A text can have more than one purpose. Choose the MAIN one. A persuasive text still uses facts, and a story with a few facts is still mainly written to entertain.
ex:
“Every class should plant a spring garden. Gardens teach science, give us fresh food, and make the school beautiful. Ask your principal today!”
Persuade. An opinion (“should”), three reasons, and a call to action (“Ask your principal today!”).

“A seed needs three things to germinate: water, air, and the right temperature. When water soaks through the seed coat, the tiny plant inside begins to grow.”
Inform / explain. Facts about a real process, told in cause-and-effect order, with no opinion.

“The airship dropped twenty feet in one second. Kate grabbed the rail and laughed. ‘Is that all you’ve got, storm?’”
Entertain. A character, a dangerous problem, dialogue, and suspense.

“The old garden was a tangle of gray branches, damp brown leaves, and vines that clung to the walls like cold fingers.”
Describe. Sight and touch details and a simile help you picture the setting; nothing is argued or taught.

An article tells how airships were invented, gives dates and inventors, then ends: “We should build airships again because they use less fuel than planes.”
Main purpose: inform; second purpose: persuade. Most of the text gives facts; only the ending gives an opinion with a reason.

check.question: “Three Ways to Keep Your Seedlings Alive: First, water the soil when the top feels dry. Next, place the pot in a sunny window. Finally, turn the pot every day so the stems grow straight.” What is the author’s main purpose?
check.answer: To explain / inform: it teaches how to care for seedlings in steps (first, next, finally). There is no story and no opinion to argue.

anchorCharts.imageAlt: Author's Purpose anchor chart poster. The study guide below explains each part with five worked examples.

anchorCharts.name: Text Structure
anchorCharts.body: Text structure is the way an author organizes information. Nonfiction often uses one of five structures. Signal words are clues, but the real test is how the ideas connect. Stories, plays, and poems have structures too: chapters, scenes, and stanzas fit together to build the whole work (RL.5.5).

guide.label: Description
guide.text: A topic and its details or features. Signal words: for example, such as, including, also, in addition.

guide.label: Sequence / Chronological
guide.text: Events or steps in time order. Signal words: first, next, then, after, finally, dates and times.

guide.label: Compare & Contrast
guide.text: How two things are alike and different. Signal words: both, similarly, like, however, but, unlike, on the other hand.

guide.label: Cause & Effect
guide.text: Why something happens (cause) and what happens as a result (effect). Signal words: because, so, as a result, therefore, since.

guide.label: Problem & Solution
guide.text: A problem is described, then one or more ways to solve it. Signal words: problem, challenge, solve, solution, one answer is.

guide.label: Chapters · Scenes · Stanzas
guide.text: Literary structure: chapters build a novel, scenes build a play, stanzas build a poem. Each part adds something: a new event, a change in setting, or a new idea.

steps: Find the topic. Then ask: what is the author mostly doing with it?
Circle signal words, but check that they match the whole passage, not just one sentence.
Sketch a quick organizer: a web, a timeline, a Venn diagram, cause → effect arrows, or problem → solution boxes.
Explain WHY the author chose that structure: it helps the reader follow steps, compare, or understand a result.
anchorCharts.tip: One “because” does not make a whole passage cause and effect. Choose the structure that organizes MOST of the text.
ex:
“First, soak the bean seeds overnight. Next, plant them two centimeters deep. After about a week, a curled shoot pushes up through the soil.”
Sequence. Steps in time order: first, next, after about a week.

“Both airships and airplanes carry passengers. However, an airship floats because it is filled with a light gas, while an airplane needs wings and speed to stay up.”
Compare & contrast. “Both” shows a likeness; “however” and “while” show differences.

“Because the spring rains came late, the soil stayed dry. As a result, many seeds did not sprout until May.”
Cause & effect. Late rain (cause) → dry soil → late sprouting (effects).

“Rabbits kept eating the school’s lettuce. The students solved the problem by building a fence of chicken wire around the beds.”
Problem & solution. A problem (rabbits) is followed by how it was fixed (a fence).

A play has three scenes: Scene 1, Mary finds a locked garden; Scene 2, she discovers the key; Scene 3, the garden blooms.
Scenes as structure. Each scene moves the plot forward: problem → discovery → resolution (RL.5.5).

check.question: “Hot-air balloons and airships both float because they are lighter than the air around them. Unlike a balloon, however, an airship has engines and can be steered.” Which structure is this?
check.answer: Compare and contrast: “both” shows how they are alike, and “unlike” and “however” show how they are different.

anchorCharts.imageAlt: Text Structure anchor chart poster. The study guide below explains each part with five worked examples.

anchorCharts.name: Theme
anchorCharts.body: The theme is the message or life lesson of a story, play, or poem. It is written as a full sentence that could be true for many people, not just one character. Find it by watching how characters respond to challenges and what they learn, or, in a poem, how the speaker reflects on a topic (RL.5.2).

guide.label: Topic ≠ Theme
guide.text: A topic is one or two words (courage, friendship). A theme is a full sentence about that topic: “Courage means acting even when you are afraid.”

guide.label: Challenge
guide.text: What problem does the main character face?

guide.label: Response
guide.text: How does the character respond? What choices does he or she make?

guide.label: Outcome & Change
guide.text: What happens because of those choices? How has the character changed by the end?

guide.label: Lesson
guide.text: What does the character learn, and what can the reader learn too? Turn it into a sentence that works for anyone.

steps: Name the topic in one or two words.
Track the challenge → response → outcome → change.
Write the theme as a full sentence without character names (use people, we, or you).
Prove it with two details from the beginning AND the end of the text.
anchorCharts.tip: Don’t retell the plot (“Mary found a garden”) and don’t write only a topic (“nature”). A theme also isn’t one character’s action; it is a lesson for everyone.
ex:
A lonely, angry girl secretly cares for a dying garden. As the plants grow, she makes friends and becomes kind.
Theme: Caring for something outside yourself can help you grow too. Topic: growth, friendship.

A cabin boy is afraid of heights, but when a stranger’s balloon is in trouble, he climbs out to help and saves the man.
Theme: Courage means doing the right thing even when you are afraid.

A boy tries to write a poem for a contest. Each version fails, but he keeps adding lines until it becomes his best work.
Theme: Mistakes and hard work are part of creating something good.

Poem: the speaker watches a frozen pond, then sees the first green buds and hears returning birds in spring.
Theme (speaker reflects): After hard times, hope and new beginnings always return.

Two friends argue over who will lead a class play. The show goes badly until they agree to share the job.
Theme: People can achieve more by working together than by competing.

check.question: Leo laughs at his grandmother’s old-fashioned stories. When he gets lost on a hike, he remembers her advice about following the stream downhill, and he finds his way home. Write the theme, not the topic.
check.answer: Sample: “The wisdom of older people can be valuable, even if it seems old-fashioned.” The topic is respect or wisdom; the theme is the full lesson Leo learns.

anchorCharts.imageAlt: Theme anchor chart poster. The study guide below explains each part with five worked examples.

anchorCharts.name: Figurative Language
anchorCharts.body: Figurative language uses words in an unusual way to create a picture or feeling. The words do NOT mean exactly what they say (that would be literal). For each example: name it → explain what it really means → tell why the author used it (RL.5.4, L.5.5).

guide.label: Simile
guide.text: Compares two unlike things using like or as. “The airship floated like a silver whale.”

guide.label: Metaphor
guide.text: Compares by saying one thing IS another, without like or as. “The garden was a sleeping giant.”

guide.label: Personification
guide.text: Gives human actions or feelings to an animal, object, or idea. “The wind tugged at my sleeve.”

guide.label: Hyperbole
guide.text: A huge exaggeration for effect, not meant to be believed. “I’ve told you a million times!”

guide.label: Idiom
guide.text: A saying whose meaning can’t be figured out from the words. “Break a leg!” means “Good luck!”

guide.label: Sound devices
guide.text: Alliteration repeats beginning sounds (“silent, silver sky”). Onomatopoeia names a sound (buzz, creak, whoosh).

steps: Notice a phrase that can’t be literally true.
Name the type: look for like/as (simile), is/was (metaphor), human actions (personification), exaggeration (hyperbole), or a saying (idiom).
Explain the real meaning in plain words.
Explain the effect: what does it make you picture or feel?
anchorCharts.tip: Not every “like” is a simile: “I like apples” compares nothing. A simile compares two DIFFERENT kinds of things: “Her voice was like a bell.”
ex:
“The clouds swallowed the airship whole.”
Personification / metaphor. Clouds can’t swallow; it means the ship disappeared completely into thick clouds. It makes the clouds seem huge and dangerous.

“The tendrils clung to the wall like tiny green hands.”
Simile (uses like). The curly stems hold on tightly, the way small hands would grip.

“Colin’s room was a prison.”
Metaphor. The room is not a real prison; it shows that Colin feels trapped and lonely there.

“This suitcase weighs a ton!”
Hyperbole. It doesn’t really weigh 1,000 kg; the speaker means it is very heavy and shows how tired he is.

“Mom said I was skating on thin ice when I came home late.”
Idiom. “Skating on thin ice” means being close to getting in trouble; it has nothing to do with real ice.

check.question: “The old floorboards groaned as we tiptoed through the silent house.” Name the figurative language and explain its effect.
check.answer: Personification: floorboards can’t groan like a person, so the creaking sounds tired and spooky. It builds a nervous, mysterious mood.

anchorCharts.imageAlt: Figurative Language anchor chart poster. The study guide below explains each part with five worked examples.

anchorCharts.name: Character
anchorCharts.body: Authors reveal characters directly (the narrator tells you: “Mary was rude”) and indirectly (you infer from what the character does and says). Use the S.T.E.A.L. clues to describe a character’s traits, feelings, motivations, and changes, and compare characters using specific details (RL.5.3).

guide.label: S · Speech
guide.text: What does the character say, and how? (shouts, whispers, teases)

guide.label: T · Thoughts
guide.text: What does the character think, wish, or worry about?

guide.label: E · Effect on others
guide.text: How do other characters react to him or her? Do they trust, fear, or avoid this person?

guide.label: A · Actions
guide.text: What does the character do, especially when facing a problem?

guide.label: L · Looks
guide.text: What does the character look like? Clothes, face, and body language (a frown, slumped shoulders).

guide.label: Trait · Feeling · Motivation
guide.text: Trait = what someone is like most of the time (stubborn, loyal). Feeling = an emotion right now (nervous). Motivation = why the character acts (wants a friend, wants to be brave).

steps: Collect S.T.E.A.L. clues from the text.
Infer a trait word that fits several clues (curious, not just “nice”).
Track change: what is the character like at the beginning and at the end, and what caused the change?
To compare two characters, put the same kind of clue side by side: how each one reacts to the same problem.
anchorCharts.tip: A feeling is not a trait. Someone who is angry once isn’t an angry person. A trait shows up again and again in the character’s actions and words.
ex:
“Mary stamped her foot. ‘I won’t go! You can’t make me!’”
Trait: stubborn / spoiled. Clues: Speech (“You can’t make me”) and Action (stamped her foot).

“Matt glanced at the dark sky, then climbed the ladder anyway, gripping each rung until his knuckles were white.”
Feeling: afraid. Trait: brave. White knuckles show fear (Looks); climbing anyway shows courage (Action).

“Whenever Dickon walked into the garden, the robin flew down to his shoulder and the other children stopped arguing.”
Trait: gentle and calming. Clue: Effect on others; animals and people relax around him.

Beginning: Colin refuses to leave his bed. Ending: he walks through the garden and laughs with his friends.
Character change: from fearful and hopeless to confident and hopeful, caused by fresh air and friendship.

Compare: when the storm hits, Nell rushes to tie down the cover, but Owen hides in the cabin and pretends to sleep.
Contrast (RL.5.3): both face the same problem; Nell is responsible and brave, while Owen avoids danger.

check.question: “Ava handed her last cookie to the new student, then quietly sat back down without saying a word about it.” What trait does this show, and which S.T.E.A.L. clues prove it?
check.answer: Generous and modest. Action: she gives away her last cookie. Speech: she says nothing about it, so she isn’t showing off.

anchorCharts.imageAlt: Character anchor chart poster. The study guide below explains each part with five worked examples.

anchorCharts.name: Literary Elements
anchorCharts.body: Literary elements are the parts every story or play is built from: characters, setting, conflict, plot, and the narrator’s point of view. Genre changes how these elements are used. That is the Module 2 big question: How does genre affect the way a story is told?

guide.label: Characters
guide.text: The people or animals in the story. The main character (protagonist) faces the problem; an antagonist works against him or her.

guide.label: Setting
guide.text: Where and when the story happens. A setting can cause the problem (a storm) or create a mood (a dark, quiet house).

guide.label: Conflict
guide.text: The main problem. Character vs. character, vs. nature, vs. society, or vs. self (an inner struggle).

guide.label: Plot
guide.text: Exposition (introduce characters and setting) → rising action → climax (turning point) → falling action → resolution.

guide.label: Point of View
guide.text: Who tells the story. First person (I, we: a character tells it) or third person (he, she, they: an outside narrator).

guide.label: Genre
guide.text: Fantasy/adventure (exciting action, unusual worlds), realistic fiction, myth, drama (dialogue and stage directions), poetry. Each genre tells a story in a different way.

steps: Name the main character and the setting (time and place).
Identify the conflict and its type.
Put the key events on a plot mountain and mark the climax.
Explain how the resolution settles the conflict and how the genre shaped the telling.
anchorCharts.tip: The climax is the TURNING POINT where the conflict is decided, not just the loudest moment. Everything after it is falling action and resolution.
ex:
“High above the clouds in 1910, the airship Aurora hummed through the night.”
Setting: in the sky, at night, in 1910. It suggests an adventure far from help.

“Nell had to choose: tell the captain she broke the compass, or let the cook take the blame.”
Conflict: character vs. self. Nell struggles with an inner choice about honesty.

“The storm tore the sail loose, and the ship began to spin toward the sea.”
Conflict: character vs. nature. The storm is the force the characters must fight.

Mary finds a key (rising action), opens the hidden door (climax: the turning point), and plants seeds with Dickon (falling action); by summer the garden is alive (resolution).
Plot mapped onto the plot mountain.

“I gripped the rail and stared down at the waves.” vs. “Matt gripped the rail and stared down at the waves.”
Point of view: the first uses I (first person); the second uses Matt (third person).

check.question: Sam is too shy to sing in the school show. He practices in front of his dog every night. On show night his hands shake, but he steps onto the stage and sings his solo. Afterward, he signs up for choir. Which event is the climax, and what type of conflict is it?
check.answer: Climax: Sam steps onto the stage and sings. That is the turning point where his problem is decided. Conflict: character vs. self, because his struggle is with his own shyness. Signing up for choir is the resolution.

anchorCharts.imageAlt: Literary Elements anchor chart poster. The study guide below explains each part with five worked examples.

anchorCharts.name: Elements of Poetry
anchorCharts.body: A poem is built from lines grouped into stanzas. Poets use sound (rhyme, rhythm, repetition) and images (sensory and figurative language) to share a feeling or idea. The speaker is the voice in the poem; it is not always the poet. Stanzas fit together to build the poem’s meaning (RL.5.5).

guide.label: Line & Stanza
guide.text: A line is one row of words. A stanza is a group of lines, like a paragraph in a poem.

guide.label: Rhyme & Rhyme Scheme
guide.text: Rhyme: words that end with the same sound (night/light). Rhyme scheme: the pattern of rhymes at line ends, labeled with letters (AABB, ABAB).

guide.label: Rhythm & Meter
guide.text: Rhythm is the beat you hear when you read aloud. Meter is a regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.

guide.label: Repetition & Refrain
guide.text: Repetition repeats words or sounds for emphasis. A refrain is a line or stanza repeated regularly, like a song’s chorus.

guide.label: Imagery & Figurative Language
guide.text: Words that appeal to the five senses, plus simile, metaphor, personification, alliteration, and onomatopoeia.

guide.label: Speaker · Form
guide.text: The speaker is the voice telling the poem. Forms include rhyming poems, free verse (no regular rhyme or meter), narrative poems (tell a story), and limericks.

steps: Read the poem aloud twice and listen for the beat and the rhymes.
Count the stanzas and lines; label the rhyme scheme with letters.
Mark repeated words or a refrain and ask why they are repeated.
Find the strongest images; decide what the speaker feels and what the poem’s theme is.
anchorCharts.tip: Label the rhyme scheme by SOUND, not spelling: “through” and “blue” rhyme, but “cough” and “dough” do not. A new sound always gets the next letter.
ex:
“The rain begins to fall (A) / Upon the garden wall (A) / The seeds wake up below (B) / And start to stretch and grow (B)”
Rhyme scheme: AABB. Lines 1-2 rhyme (fall/wall); lines 3-4 rhyme (below/grow).

“The moon’s a lamp so bright (A) / That hangs above the town (B) / It shines all through the night (A) / Until the sun comes down (B)”
ABAB rhyme scheme (bright/night, town/down), and a metaphor: the moon IS a lamp.

Every stanza of a poem ends with “And still the poem goes on and on.”
Refrain. The repeated line ties the stanzas together and makes the poem feel endless.

“Splash! Drip, drip. The puddles plop / as raindrops tap the tin roof top.”
Onomatopoeia (splash, drip, plop, tap) creates the sound of rain; the rhyme plop/top gives it a bouncy rhythm.

“I stand by the window. / Snow falls without a sound. / I wait for my father’s car.”
Free verse (no rhyme or set beat). The speaker is a child waiting; the quiet imagery shows loneliness and hope.

check.question: “A cat sat on a mat, (A) / Wearing a tiny hat. (?) / It purred a happy tune, (?) / And napped all afternoon. (?)” Write the rhyme scheme.
check.answer: AABB: mat/hat share the A sound; tune/afternoon share a new B sound.

anchorCharts.imageAlt: Elements of Poetry anchor chart poster. The study guide below explains each part with five worked examples.

anchorCharts.name: Elements of Drama
anchorCharts.body: A drama, or play, is a story written to be performed. Readers learn almost everything through dialogue and stage directions instead of a narrator.

guide.label: Cast of characters
guide.text: The list at the beginning that names each character and often describes them.

guide.label: Dialogue
guide.text: The words the characters speak. Each line begins with the speaker’s name, with no quotation marks.

guide.label: Stage directions
guide.text: Italic words, usually in parentheses, that tell actors how to move or speak and describe the setting, sound, and lighting.

guide.label: Scenes and acts
guide.text: Plays are divided into scenes (and sometimes acts). A new scene often means a change in time or place.

guide.label: Setting description
guide.text: Stage directions at the start of a scene that describe the time, place, and set.

steps: Read the cast list to learn who is who.
Read the stage directions carefully; they show feelings and actions the dialogue does not say.
Compare scenes to see how time, place, and characters change.
anchorCharts.tip: Stage directions are not spoken aloud. A character’s feelings may be shown only in a direction like (with contempt) or (eyes shining).
ex: In The Garden Behind the Wall, (with contempt) tells the actor playing Rosa to say “This whole place is dead” scornfully.
Scene 1 is early spring with dead vines; Scene 2 is six weeks later with roses on the wall. The scene change shows time passing and the garden’s recovery.

check.question: “SAM: (slamming the door) Fine. I don’t care anyway.” What does the stage direction suggest that the words alone do not?
check.answer: Slamming the door shows Sam is angry or upset, so “I don’t care” probably is not true. The direction reveals his real feelings.

anchorCharts.name: Text Evidence
anchorCharts.body: Text evidence is a specific detail from the text that supports an answer. You can quote exactly or paraphrase accurately.

guide.label: Answer
guide.text: Make a clear statement that answers the question.

guide.label: Evidence
guide.text: Choose a relevant action, fact, line, or stage direction. Name the paragraph, scene, or stanza when helpful.

guide.label: Explain
guide.text: Show how the detail supports your answer: “This shows … because …”.

steps: Underline the important words in the question.
Return to the text and choose the strongest matching detail.
Connect the evidence to your answer in your own words.
anchorCharts.tip: In “Which sentence best supports…” questions, several choices may be true. Pick the one that PROVES the idea in the question, not just one that is about the same topic.
ex: Answer: Grandma Ines has changed. Evidence: “I have been sitting still for far too long. Bring me that packet of seeds.” Explanation: she was always in her chair, and now she joins the work.
To show that dormancy protects a seed, use “the next hard frost would kill the tender young plant,” not a sentence that only defines dormancy.

check.question: Question: Is Captain Osei calm? Text: “The captain did not panic. ‘Every hand I have is holding this ship steady,’ he said.” Write an answer with evidence.
check.answer: Yes, Captain Osei is calm. The text says he “did not panic,” and he explains the situation clearly instead of shouting, even in a storm.

anchorCharts.imageAlt: Text Evidence illustrated anchor chart. The study guide below explains the concepts and examples.

anchorCharts.name: Vocabulary in Context
anchorCharts.body: Use nearby words, sentences, and events to infer the meaning of an unfamiliar word. Then test that meaning in the sentence.

guide.label: Definition or restatement
guide.text: “A seed begins to grow, or germinate…” The words after “or” give the meaning.

guide.label: Example
guide.text: “A plant without enough nitrogen often develops pale yellow leaves.” The example explains deficiency as a lack.

guide.label: Contrast
guide.text: “The vines are matted on top, but look underneath.” The contrast hints at a thick, tangled surface.

guide.label: Situation
guide.text: Nell grips the rail at the first post before moving on. Her actions explain hesitated: paused because she was unsure or afraid.

steps: Read before and after the unfamiliar word.
Find a clue and suggest a meaning that fits the context.
Substitute your meaning and reread; check word parts if useful.
anchorCharts.tip: Choose the meaning used in THIS text. “Project” can mean a school assignment or to throw a light or voice outward.
ex: In How a Seed Wakes Up, seeds planted too densely “crowd one another.” The clue shows densely means packed closely together.
“A seed begins to grow… only when conditions are favorable” and then lists what it needs. Favorable means helpful or just right.

check.question: “The kitten was restless; it paced, pawed at the door, and would not settle on its blanket.” What does restless mean, and what is the clue?
check.answer: Restless means unable to stay still or relax. Pacing, pawing, and refusing to settle all show it cannot rest.

anchorCharts.imageAlt: Vocabulary in Context illustrated anchor chart. The study guide below explains the concepts and examples.

passages.title: Storm over the Kestrel
passages.body: Original practice story written in the style of an adventure novel. Paragraphs are numbered. 1 The airship Kestrel hummed over the dark ocean like a giant bee that had lost its way home. From the small round porthole beside her bunk, Nell Varga could see nothing below but black water and, now and then, the white scribble of a wave. She was twelve years old and the youngest crew member aboard, and her job was simple: polish the brass, carry messages, and stay out of the way. 2 Tonight she was restless. The wind had been growling at the hull since supper, and the floor kept tilting beneath her feet. Something about the sky felt wrong, as if the clouds were holding their breath. 3 A loud crack split the air. Nell pressed her face to the glass. Far back along the outer catwalk, a dark shape flapped and twisted in the wind. It was the canvas cover over the cargo hold, and one of its fastenings had snapped. If the cover tore away, rain would pour onto the contents of the hold: three hundred crates of medicine bound for the island hospital at Port Ivy. 4 Nell ran to the bridge. Captain Osei stood at the wheel, his watchful eyes fixed on the storm ahead. "The cargo cover is loose!" she gasped. 5 The captain did not panic. "Every hand I have is holding this ship steady," he said. "Mr. Lund will go as soon as he can be spared." 6 "There isn't time," Nell said. "I'm small. I can clip onto the safety line." 7 For a long moment, the captain studied her. Then he nodded once. "Clip on, keep low, and come back the instant I call. That is an order." 8 The catwalk was a narrow ribbon of metal stretched along the side of the ship. The wind seized Nell's jacket and tried to drag her into the sky. Her heart hammered. At the first post she hesitated, gripping the rail so tightly that her knuckles turned white. Below her, the ocean waited like an open mouth. 9 She thought of the hospital at Port Ivy and of the children who would wake up tomorrow needing the medicine in those crates. She took one breath, then another, and inched forward. 10 The loose cover cracked like a whip above her head. On her first attempt to grab its corner, the canvas jerked free and slapped her shoulder. On her second, she caught it and pulled with all her weight. Rain stung her face. Her arms burned. At last she looped the rope through the iron ring, tied the knot her father had taught her, and tugged it tight. The cover lay flat and still. 11 When Nell stumbled back onto the bridge, soaked and shaking, the captain did not scold her. He handed her a towel and a cup of warm tea. "Tomorrow," he said, "you'll learn to tie the storm knots properly. A crew is only as strong as its smallest member." 12 Through the porthole, the first gray light of morning was creeping over the clouds. Nell smiled. For the first time since she had come aboard, she felt that the Kestrel truly belonged to her, too.

questions.q: Which choice best describes the setting of the story?
choices: A busy island hospital on a sunny morning
A ship's cargo hold during a calm night at sea
An airship flying over the ocean at night during a storm
A harbor where an airship is being repaired

questions.q: What is the main conflict in the story?
choices: Nell must secure the loose cargo cover before the storm ruins the medicine.
Nell and Captain Osei argue about who should steer the airship.
Mr. Lund refuses to help Nell polish the brass.
The hospital at Port Ivy does not want the medicine.

questions.q: Which event is the climax of the story?
choices: Nell hears a loud crack and sees the cover flapping (paragraph 3).
The captain gives Nell permission to go onto the catwalk (paragraph 7).
The captain hands Nell a towel and a cup of tea (paragraph 11).
On her second attempt, Nell catches the canvas and ties it down (paragraph 10).

questions.q: In paragraph 1, the author writes that the airship "hummed over the dark ocean like a giant bee that had lost its way home." What does this simile suggest?
choices: The airship is covered in yellow and black stripes.
The airship makes a steady buzzing sound and seems small and alone over the huge ocean.
The crew of the airship is lost and cannot find Port Ivy.
The airship moves quickly from flower to flower.

questions.q: In paragraph 8, "Below her, the ocean waited like an open mouth." How does this sentence affect the mood of the story?
choices: It makes the scene feel peaceful and calm.
It shows that Nell is hungry after her long night.
It builds suspense by making the ocean seem hungry and dangerous.
It explains how deep the ocean is below the ship.

questions.q: Read this sentence from paragraph 8: "At the first post she hesitated, gripping the rail so tightly that her knuckles turned white." What does hesitated mean?
choices: Paused because she felt unsure or afraid
Ran ahead without thinking
Shouted for help
Slipped and almost fell

questions.q: Which sentence from the story best explains why Nell keeps moving forward on the catwalk?
choices: "The catwalk was a narrow ribbon of metal stretched along the side of the ship."
"Her heart hammered."
"Rain stung her face."
"She thought of the hospital at Port Ivy and of the children who would wake up tomorrow needing the medicine in those crates."

questions.q: Which word best describes Captain Osei, based on paragraphs 4-7 and 11?
choices: Careless, because he sends a child outside without any rules
Calm and fair, because he stays steady in the storm and trusts Nell with clear safety orders
Angry, because he scolds Nell when she returns
Nervous, because he cannot decide what to do

questions.q: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
choices: Airships are dangerous and should not fly in storms.
Children should always stay out of the way of adults.
Courage means acting to help others even when you are afraid.
Medicine is the most important cargo a ship can carry.

questions.q: How does Nell change from the beginning of the story to the end? Use one detail from the beginning and one from the end.
questions.sampleAnswer: At the beginning, Nell feels like an outsider whose job is to "stay out of the way." By the end, after bravely tying down the cargo cover, the captain praises her and she feels that the Kestrel "truly belonged to her, too." She changes from feeling unimportant to feeling like a real member of the crew.

passages.title: The Garden Behind the Wall
passages.body: Original practice play. Read the cast list and the stage directions (in italics and parentheses) carefully. The Garden Behind the Wall A Play in Two Scenes CAST OF CHARACTERS ROSA, an eleven-year-old girl who has just moved in with her grandmother GRANDMA INES, Rosa's grandmother, who rarely leaves her chair by the window THEO, a boy from next door who loves growing things SCENE 1 (Early spring. A yard behind an old stone house. Dead brown vines cover a high wall. A rusty gate hangs open. ROSA kicks at a pile of dry leaves.) ROSA: (with contempt) This whole place is dead. Even the weeds have given up. THEO: (peering over the wall) It isn't dead. It's sleeping. ROSA: (startled, spinning around) Who are you? Were you spying on me? THEO: I'm Theo. I live next door. (He climbs over the wall and kneels beside it. He pulls back a clump of tangled stems.) See? The vines are matted on top, but look underneath. ROSA: (leaning closer, curious in spite of herself) It's green. There's a tiny green tendril curling around the stem! THEO: Your grandpa planted this garden. After he died, nobody touched it for three years. ROSA: (quietly) Grandma never talks about him. She just sits by the window all day. THEO: Maybe the garden could talk for her. (ROSA hesitates. Then she picks up a rusty rake leaning against the gate and begins to pull away the dead leaves. Lights fade.) SCENE 2 (Six weeks later. The same yard, now cleared. Rows of young plants line the beds. Pink roses climb the wall. Birds sing. ROSA and THEO are digging. GRANDMA INES appears in the doorway, leaning on a cane.) GRANDMA INES: (in a shaky voice) What have you done? ROSA: (dropping her trowel, nervous) I'm sorry, Grandma. I should have asked. We found Grandpa's notebook in the shed. He scrawled the name of every plant on the first page, so we knew what to look for. (GRANDMA INES walks slowly down the steps. She touches a rose as if it were made of glass.) GRANDMA INES: He planted these the year your mother was born. I thought they had died with him. THEO: They only needed someone to wake them up. GRANDMA INES: (turning to ROSA, her eyes shining) When you came here, you were as gray as this yard. Now look at you. You have dirt on your nose and sunshine in your face. ROSA: (laughing and wiping her nose) Will you help us, Grandma? You must know where everything belongs. GRANDMA INES: (lowering herself onto the garden bench and reaching for a trowel) I have been sitting still for far too long. Bring me that packet of seeds. (The three work side by side as the lights slowly grow brighter. Curtain.)

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the Cast of Characters at the beginning of the play?
choices: To tell how the play will end
To describe the setting of Scene 2
To give the actors' lines in order
To introduce who the characters are before the action begins

questions.q: In Scene 1, Rosa says, (with contempt) "This whole place is dead." What does with contempt tell the actor playing Rosa to do?
choices: Say the line with scorn, as if the garden is worthless
Whisper the line kindly to Theo
Shout the line with joy
Say the line while crying

questions.q: Read the stage direction: (leaning closer, curious in spite of herself). What does it reveal about Rosa at this moment?
choices: She is angry that Theo climbed over the wall.
She is starting to become interested in the garden, even though she did not want to be.
She is afraid the vines will hurt her.
She already knows everything about plants.

questions.q: Theo says, "The vines are matted on top, but look underneath." Which meaning of matted fits this line?
choices: Brightly colored
Neatly trimmed
Thickly tangled together
Freshly planted

questions.q: Why does the playwright divide the play into two scenes?
choices: To introduce a new set of characters in Scene 2
To show that time has passed and the garden and characters have changed
To move the story to a different country
To give the audience a break before the climax

questions.q: Theo says, "It isn't dead. It's sleeping." What does this line show about Theo?
choices: He is hopeful and can see possibilities that others miss.
He is lazy and does not want to work in the garden.
He wants to trick Rosa.
He thinks the garden should be torn down.

questions.q: Grandma Ines tells Rosa, "When you came here, you were as gray as this yard." What does this simile suggest about Rosa when she first arrived?
choices: She was wearing gray clothes.
She was covered in dust from the yard.
She was unhappy and lifeless, like the neglected garden.
She was older than she looked.

questions.q: Which line from Scene 2 best supports the idea that Grandma Ines has changed?
choices: "What have you done?"
"He planted these the year your mother was born."
"I thought they had died with him."
"I have been sitting still for far too long. Bring me that packet of seeds."

questions.q: Which statement best expresses a theme of the play?
choices: Old houses should always be repaired.
Bringing something back to life can help people heal and grow closer.
Children should never touch things without asking.
Gardens need water and sunlight to grow.

questions.q: How does Rosa change from Scene 1 to Scene 2? Use one stage direction and one line of dialogue in your answer.
questions.sampleAnswer: In Scene 1, Rosa is bitter about her new home; the stage direction (with contempt) shows she says "This whole place is dead" scornfully. By Scene 2 she has worked hard to bring the garden back, and she happily asks, "Will you help us, Grandma?" (laughing and wiping her nose). She changes from scornful and unhappy to hopeful, caring, and connected to her grandmother.

passages.title: How a Seed Wakes Up
passages.body: An informational article. Paragraphs are numbered. How a Seed Wakes Up 1 All winter long, a seed can lie in the cold ground looking as lifeless as a pebble. Yet inside its hard coat, a tiny plant is waiting. When the season changes, that plant will awaken and push its way toward the light. How does a seed know when it is time to grow? The answer lies in a series of signals from its surroundings. Waiting for the Right Moment 2 A seed has three main parts. The seed coat is a tough outer layer that protects everything inside. The embryo is the baby plant. The endosperm, or stored food, gives the embryo energy until it can make its own. These contents allow a seed to survive for months, or even years, without growing at all. This resting state is called dormancy. 3 Dormancy protects the seed. If a seed sprouted during a warm week in December, the next hard frost would kill the tender young plant. Therefore, many seeds will not grow until they have gone through a long stretch of cold. The cold works like a calendar, telling the seed that winter has truly passed. The Signals of Spring 4 A seed begins to grow, or germinate, only when conditions are favorable. It needs three things: water, oxygen, and the right temperature. In spring, melting snow and rain soak the soil. Because the seed coat absorbs this water, the seed swells and its coat splits open. At the same time, warmer soil speeds up the chemical changes inside the seed. From Seed to Seedling 5 Germination follows a predictable order. First, the root pushes downward. It anchors the plant and begins drawing water from the soil. Next, a shoot curls upward toward the surface. Once the shoot breaks through the soil, its first leaves unfold. Finally, the leaves begin to use sunlight to make food, a process called photosynthesis. The stored food is used up, and the seedling now feeds itself. When Things Go Wrong 6 Not every seed succeeds. If seeds are planted too densely, the seedlings crowd one another and compete for water and light, so many grow weak and thin. A seedling may also suffer from a deficiency of nutrients. For example, a plant without enough nitrogen often develops pale yellow leaves. Gardeners prevent these problems by spacing seeds carefully and enriching the soil with compost. 7 It is reasonable to think of spring as one sudden change, but for a seed, it is a careful chain of events. Each step depends on the one before it. The next time you notice green shoots poking through the soil, remember that each one waited, tested its world, and began at exactly the right moment.

questions.q: What is the author's main purpose for writing this article?
choices: To persuade readers to plant a garden this spring
To entertain readers with a story about a seed
To compare winter and summer weather
To explain how and why seeds begin to grow in spring

questions.q: Which text structure does the author use in paragraph 5?
choices: Sequence, because it tells the stages of germination in order
Compare and contrast, because it shows how roots and shoots are alike
Problem and solution, because it explains how gardeners fix weak plants
Description, because it lists the three parts of a seed

questions.q: According to paragraph 4, what happens because the seed coat absorbs water?
choices: The soil becomes warmer.
The seed swells and its coat splits open.
The seed goes into dormancy.
The leaves begin photosynthesis.

questions.q: Which sentence from the article best supports the idea that dormancy helps a seed survive?
choices: "The embryo is the baby plant."
"This resting state is called dormancy."
"If a seed sprouted during a warm week in December, the next hard frost would kill the tender young plant."
"In spring, melting snow and rain soak the soil."

questions.q: Why does the author write that "the cold works like a calendar" in paragraph 3?
choices: To help readers understand that a long cold period tells the seed when winter is over
To show that seeds can read dates
To persuade readers that winter is the best season
To describe what a calendar looks like

questions.q: In paragraph 4, a seed grows "only when conditions are favorable." Which phrase from the paragraph best helps you understand favorable?
choices: "melting snow and rain soak the soil"
"its coat splits open"
"chemical changes inside the seed"
"It needs three things: water, oxygen, and the right temperature."

questions.q: In paragraph 6, seeds planted too densely "crowd one another." What does densely mean?
choices: Deep under the soil
Packed closely together
Very slowly
In bright sunlight

questions.q: Read the sentences: "A seedling may also suffer from a deficiency of nutrients. For example, a plant without enough nitrogen often develops pale yellow leaves." What does deficiency mean?
choices: An extra supply
A strong smell
A lack or shortage
A bright color

questions.q: How does the heading "When Things Go Wrong" help the reader?
choices: It signals that paragraph 6 will describe problems seeds can face and how gardeners prevent them.
It tells the reader that the article is a story with a sad ending.
It shows that the author is about to list the parts of a seed.
It explains the meaning of germinate.

questions.q: Explain what happens to a seed from the moment it absorbs water until the seedling can feed itself. Use at least three steps from the article, in order.
questions.sampleAnswer: First, the seed coat absorbs water, so the seed swells and the coat splits open. Then the root pushes downward to anchor the plant and draw water. Next, a shoot curls upward and breaks through the soil, and its first leaves unfold. Finally, the leaves use sunlight to make food through photosynthesis, so the seedling feeds itself.

passages.title: Three Poems: Ditties, Gardens, and Rain
passages.body: Three original poems. Read each poem aloud to hear its rhythm and sounds. Lines in italics are a refrain. Poem 1: The Ditty That Wouldn't Quit On Monday, Bartholomew learned a new ditty, A silly old tune about Pete and his kitty. He hummed it at breakfast, he hummed it at nine, He hummed it while waiting in the lunchroom line. Oh, tum-tiddle-tee and a tum-tiddle-toe, Once it gets started, it won't let you go! His teacher said, "Bart, could you hush for a while?" His sister just groaned with a sour little smile. The dog howled along with a long, wobbly "Woo!" The kettle went whistling. It sang the song, too! Oh, tum-tiddle-tee and a tum-tiddle-toe, Once it gets started, it won't let you go! He tried to restrain it; he pressed his lips tight, But it buzzed in his bones like a bee in the night. He scrawled it on paper and buried it deep, But it climbed out and sang to him all through his sleep. Oh, tum-tiddle-tee and a tum-tiddle-toe, Once it gets started, it won't let you go! So now that you've read it, I'm sorry to say, You'll be humming it, too, for the rest of the day. Oh, tum-tiddle-tee and a tum-tiddle-toe, Once it gets started, it won't let you go! Poem 2: What the Garden Knows Under the frost, the garden is a closed book no one has learned to read. Then April arrives, soft-footed, knocking on the door of every seed. A tendril unrolls like a question mark, asking the sky, Is it time? The robins answer. The rain answers. The sun leans close and whispers, Yes. Poem 3: Spring Rain Pitter, patter, on the pane, Drip and drop and splash and spill, Here's the music of the rain Dancing down the windowsill. Every puddle is a drum, Every gutter hums along. Come and listen, children, come! Spring is singing her first song.

questions.q: In Poem 1, which lines are the refrain?
choices: "On Monday, Bartholomew learned a new ditty, / A silly old tune about Pete and his kitty."
"He tried to restrain it; he pressed his lips tight"

choices: ABAB

choices: The speaker tells the reader directly that the ditty will now be stuck in the reader's head, too.

The speaker describes what Pete's kitty looks like.
The speaker apologizes to Bartholomew's teacher.

questions.q: In Poem 2, "the garden is a closed book / no one has learned to read." What does this metaphor suggest?
choices: The garden is full of old books.

In winter, the life inside the garden is hidden and mysterious.
The garden is too difficult to take care of.

questions.q: Why is Poem 2 an example of free verse, while Poem 3 is not?
choices: Poem 2 has more stanzas than Poem 3.
Poem 2 uses figurative language, and Poem 3 does not.
Poem 2 is about a garden, and Poem 3 is about rain.
Poem 2 has no regular rhyme scheme or steady beat, while Poem 3 has both.

questions.q: Which line from Poem 3 contains the most onomatopoeia?
choices: "Pitter, patter, on the pane,"
"Every puddle is a drum,"
"Come and listen, children, come!"
"Spring is singing her first song."

questions.q: Which theme do Poem 2 and Poem 3 share?
choices: Rain makes it hard for children to play outside.
Spring brings new life and joy to the world.
Gardens should be kept closed during winter.
Music is more important than nature.

questions.q: Choose Poem 2 or Poem 3. Explain how the poet uses personification to describe spring. Quote at least one line from the poem.
questions.sampleAnswer: In Poem 2, the poet writes that April arrives "soft-footed, knocking on the door of every seed" and that "the sun leans close and whispers, Yes." Giving April and the sun human actions makes spring seem gentle and kind, like a friend waking the seeds up. (Poem 3: "Spring is singing her first song" and "Every gutter hums along" make spring sound joyful, like a person making music.)

passages.title: Author's Purpose and Text Structure Practice
passages.body: Practice set. Read each short excerpt, then decide the author's purpose and how the text is organized. Author's purpose: persuade (convince), inform or explain (teach facts, show how or why), entertain (tell a story or poem). Text structures: description, sequence, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution. Excerpt 1. Every family should grow at least one plant on a windowsill. Caring for a plant teaches children patience and responsibility. Fresh herbs make meals taste better. Best of all, a pot of soil and a packet of seeds cost less than a movie ticket. Start your window garden this weekend! Excerpt 2. Pea plants climb by using tendrils, thin curling stems that wrap around anything they touch. A single tendril can coil around a string in less than an hour. Tendrils help the plant lift its leaves toward the sunlight without growing a thick, heavy stem. Excerpt 3. Gus the squirrel had a plan. Every night he crept into Mrs. Patel's flowerbed, dug up one tulip bulb, and buried it in the neighbor's yard. By April, the neighbor had a mysterious row of red tulips, and Mrs. Patel had a very bare garden and a very puzzled face. Excerpt 4. To grow a bean in a jar, first fold a wet paper towel and press it against the inside of a clear jar. Next, slide a bean between the towel and the glass. Then place the jar in a warm, sunny spot. After about five days, you will witness a root poking out. Finally, watch for the first green leaves. Excerpt 5. Hot-air balloons and airships both float because they are lighter than the air around them. However, a hot-air balloon can only drift wherever the wind blows it. An airship, unlike a balloon, has engines and a rudder, so a pilot can steer it in any direction. Excerpt 6. Hydrogen is the lightest gas, but it catches fire very easily. As a result, early airships that were filled with hydrogen were dangerous to fly. For this reason, modern airships are filled with helium, a gas that does not burn. Excerpt 7. Every recess, students ran straight through the school garden and trampled the young plants. The garden club decided to take action for their spring project. They built a low wooden fence, painted bright signs, and made a stone path around the beds. Within a week, the plants were growing safely again. Excerpt 8. In September 1783, two French brothers sent a hot-air balloon into the sky carrying a sheep, a duck, and a rooster. The animals landed safely about eight minutes later. Two months after that, in November, two men made the first free flight in one of the brothers' balloons and drifted over Paris for about twenty-five minutes.

choices: To inform
To entertain
To persuade
To explain a process

To inform readers about how tulips grow
To explain how to plant tulip bulbs

choices: Sequence
Cause and effect

Description

questions.q: Excerpts 4 and 7 both describe things people do with plants, but they are organized differently. Explain the structure of each and give one clue from each excerpt.
questions.sampleAnswer: Excerpt 4 uses sequence: it gives steps in order with clue words like "first," "next," "then," and "finally." Excerpt 7 uses problem and solution: the problem is that students trampled the plants, and the solution is the fence, signs, and path the garden club built.
